name: Eyebrow growth serum
lead: Eyebrow growth serums are topical cosmetic products, often containing peptides or botanical extracts, marketed to make sparse brows look denser or fuller. They are discussed in looksmaxxing communities alongside castor oil, microneedling, minoxidil and prescription prostaglandin analogues.[1][2]

Published evidence specific to over-the-counter serums is thin. A 2019 paper in Clinical, Cosmetic and Investigational Dermatology reported on a plant-derived extract (Jarilla-Coffea) described as improving eyelash and eyebrow growth in women.[3] Studies of bimatoprost, a prescription prostaglandin analogue, have examined its use on eyebrows.[4][5]

paras: Serums are brushed or dabbed onto the brow area. Products vary widely, and some contain ingredients that forum users have catalogued from cosmetic-ingredient lists, such as myristoyl pentapeptide-17, myristoyl hexapeptide-16 and octapeptide-2, which supporters describe as stimulating hair-related keratin genes or counteracting inhibitory signals in follicles.[6]

A 2011 report in Dermatologic Surgery examined bimatoprost ophthalmic solution 0.03% for eyebrow growth.[4] A 2020 retrospective study in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology followed 48 patients with eyebrow hypotrichosis treated with bimatoprost 0.01% over 24 weeks, analysing changes in hair density and diameter by part of the brow (head, body, tail).[5] These concern a prescription drug rather than over-the-counter serums.

The 2019 Jarilla-Coffea extract paper, whose title reports improved lash and brow growth in women, is the main published study identified of a cosmetic botanical product.[3] No trial of peptide-based brow serums was found.

A looksmax.org thread lists peptide ingredients and asks members to find a serum containing them; a reply asks for a breakdown of how legitimate each is, and the original poster says they are legitimate but a good product is hard to find.[6] Another thread asks about the best microneedling approach for brow growth.[7] Castor oil is also recommended in forum answers, with one user saying shaved brows return within two to four weeks.[8]

card.summary: Peptide and botanical brow serums are popular online; published evidence centres on prescription bimatoprost, not the OTC products.
card.note: Studies of bimatoprost for brows do not apply to peptide serums.

quick.overview:
Eyebrow growth serums are topical products sold to make brows look denser. Many contain peptides or plant extracts.

Research mostly concerns prescription bimatoprost; one 2019 paper studied a botanical extract.
quick.mechanism: Makers and forum users describe peptides as stimulating hair-follicle activity. No trials of those peptide serums for brows were found.
quick.risks: Eye-area products can irritate. Bimatoprost, a prescription drug, has its own documented effects such as eyelid darkening.
